question:
A 67-year-old man comes to the emergency department for the evaluation of two episodes of red urine since this morning. He has no pain with urination. He reports lower back pain and fever. Six months ago, he was diagnosed with osteoarthritis of the right knee that he manages with 1–2 tablets of ibuprofen per day. He has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for the past 45 years. He does not drink alcohol. His temperature is 38.5°C (101.3°F), pulse is 95/min, and blood pressure is 130/80 mm Hg. Physical examination shows faint, diffuse maculopapular rash, and bilateral flank pain. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Urinalysis shows:
Blood +3
Protein +1
RBC 10–12/hpf
RBC cast negative
Eosinophils numerous
Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?"?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: NSAID use (ibuprofen) -> acute interstitial nephritis -> eosinophils in urine -> 80% CHAIN: Fever and flank pain -> systemic symptoms -> acute kidney injury -> 70% CHAIN: Hematuria (red urine) -> blood in urine -> glomerular injury -> acute glomerulonephritis -> 80%
enhanced_information: The most likely diagnosis for the 67-year-old man presenting with red urine, lower back pain, fever, and urinalysis findings of hematuria, proteinuria, and eosinophils is acute tubulointerstitial nephritis. This is supported by the chain linking NSAID use (ibuprofen) to acute interstitial nephritis, as well as the presence of eosinophils in the urine, which aligns with the standard understanding of this condition. The evidence paths further reinforce the association between ibuprofen and acute tubulointerstitial nephritis, providing additional support for this diagnosis.
analysis: The patient's presentation with red urine, lower back pain, fever, and urinalysis findings of hematuria, proteinuria, and eosinophils points towards acute tubulointerstitial nephritis. The history of NSAID use (ibuprofen) is a common cause of this condition. The presence of eosinophils in the urine further supports this diagnosis. Acute glomerulonephritis typically presents with different clinical and laboratory features. Crystal-induced acute kidney injury is less likely given the clinical context. Renal cell carcinoma is not supported by the presentation and urinalysis findings. Acute tubular necrosis usually presents differently and is less likely in this case.
